claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi and closely related high-entropy-alloy derivatives have high saturation magnetization and room-temperature coercivity at or below approximately 100 Oe.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 1–2 at.% interstitial carbon to an fcc FeCoNi-based alloy.
Adding 1–2 at.% carbon will produce nanoscale carbide-like clusters or carbon segregation at grain boundaries.
The carbon-induced clusters or segregated regions will remain incorporated within an overall fcc matrix.
Carbon-induced local chemical heterogeneities will act as magnetic-domain-wall pinning centers.
Domain-wall pinning will increase the energy barrier for domain-wall motion.
Increasing the barrier to domain-wall motion will increase the coercive field.
The carbon-modified alloy will have a coercive field significantly above approximately 100 Oe relative to a carbon-free matched control.
The carbon-modified alloy will retain high saturation magnetization with only a minimal reduction relative to the control.
Restricting carbon to 1–2 at.% will avoid extensive secondary-phase formation.
Extensive secondary-phase formation could compromise the fcc matrix and high saturation magnetization.
The spatial distribution of carbon between grain-boundary segregation and nanoprecipitate formation may vary with processing conditions.
The experiment will compare carbon-free and 1–2 at.% carbon-containing samples processed identically apart from carbon content.

TEM or atom-probe tomography will be used to assess carbon-induced nanoscale features, and room-temperature VSM or SQUID hysteresis measurements will determine coercivity and saturation magnetization.
Failure to obtain a reproducible, statistically significant coercivity increase above the approximately 100 Oe baseline while retaining high saturation magnetization will falsify the hypothesis.
